nodes.label: Architecture Decision Records
nodes.rationale: ADRs create a decision journal that explains WHY the architecture looks the way it does. Written for a future reader with no context, because the code shows what was built and only the ADR explains why.

nodes.label: ADR Creation Threshold
nodes.rationale: Create one when the decision is hard to reverse, spans teams, has cost/performance/security weight, or was debated - disagreement itself means the reasoning needs recording. Skip routine or trivially reversible choices, because granular ADRs dilute the journal.

nodes.label: Alternatives Considered Section
nodes.rationale: Omitting alternatives makes the decision look unconsidered, and omitting negative consequences creates false confidence. Being honest about trade-offs builds trust, so Positive/Negative/Neutral consequences are all mandatory.

nodes.label: ADR Lifecycle States
nodes.rationale: Proposed, Accepted, Deprecated, Superseded. Superseding is bidirectional - the new ADR links back and the old one forward - so a reader landing on a stale decision is never left following it.

nodes.label: ADR Numbering Convention
nodes.rationale: Zero-padded sequential numbers never reused even when deprecated, kebab-case suffix, one index.md listing status and a one-line summary, so a number always resolves to exactly one decision for the life of the project.

nodes.label: ADR as Decision Tool, Not Documentation
nodes.rationale: Create the ADR BEFORE implementation: it is a decision tool, not documentation. Writing ADRs after the fact is listed as the first common mistake, because a retrospective ADR cannot influence the decision it describes.
